title: Part 1, Chapter 39
paragraphs: In which the captive tells the story of his life and adventures

My family came from a village in the mountains of Leon, and nature had treated it more kindly and generously than fortune ever did. Still, amid the general poverty of those communities, my father had a reputation as a rich man — and he really would have been one, if he had been as skilled at holding on to his property as he was at spending it. This habit of being open-handed and extravagant he had picked up from serving as a soldier in his youth, because the soldier's life is a school where the miser learns to be generous and the generous man learns to be a spendthrift; any soldiers who turn out to be misers are freaks you almost never see. My father went past generosity and edged into outright extravagance, a disposition that does no good at all to a married man with children who will inherit his name and position. My father had three children, all sons, and all old enough to choose a profession. Realizing, then, that he could not fight his own nature, he decided to strip himself of the very instrument and cause of his extravagance and waste — to strip himself of his wealth, without which Alexander the Great himself would have looked stingy. So one day he called the three of us aside into a room and spoke to us in words that went roughly like this:

"My sons, to convince you that I love you, nothing more needs to be known or said than that you are my sons; and to make you suspect that I do not love you, nothing more is needed than the knowledge that I have no self-control whatsoever when it comes to preserving your inheritance. So, to make sure that from now on you can trust that I love you like a father and have no desire to ruin you like a stepfather, I intend to do with you something I have been considering for a while and have settled on after careful deliberation. You are now old enough to choose your path in life, or at least to choose a calling that will bring you honor and profit when you are older. What I have decided to do is divide my property into four parts: three I will give to you, each receiving his portion with no favoritism, and the fourth I will keep to live on and support myself for whatever remains of the life Heaven chooses to grant me. But I want each of you, when he takes possession of the share that falls to him, to follow one of the paths I am about to lay out. In this Spain of ours there is a proverb that strikes me as very true — as they all are, being short sayings distilled from long practical experience — and the one I mean goes, 'The church, or the sea, or the king's house.' Put more plainly, it means: whoever wants to prosper and grow rich should either enter the church, or go to sea and take up commerce as his trade, or enter the king's service in his household, because as they say, 'Better a king's crumb than a lord's favor.' I say this because it is my will and my wish that one of you pursue learning, another business, and the third serve the king in his wars — for getting a place in his household service is hard to manage, and while war may not bring much wealth, it brings great distinction and fame. Eight days from now I will hand each of you his full share in cash, without cheating you of a single penny, as you will see in the end. Now tell me whether you are willing to follow my idea and my advice as I have set them out for you."

He called on me, as the eldest, to answer first. After urging him not to strip himself of his property but to spend all of it however he pleased — since we were young men perfectly capable of earning our own living — I agreed to go along with his wishes, and said that mine were to take up the profession of arms and through it serve God and my king. My second brother, after making the same plea, decided to go to the Indies, investing the portion that fell to him in trade. The youngest, and in my opinion the wisest, said he would rather enter the church, or go finish his studies at Salamanca. As soon as we had reached an understanding and chosen our professions, my father embraced us all, and within the short time he had named he carried out everything he had promised. When he had given each of us his share — which, as well as I remember, was three thousand ducats apiece in cash (an uncle of ours bought the estate and paid for it on the spot, so it would not pass out of the family) — all three of us said goodbye to our good father on the same day. And at that moment, since it seemed inhuman to me to leave my father with such meager resources in his old age, I persuaded him to take back two of my three thousand ducats, because the remainder would be enough to outfit me with everything a soldier needed. My two brothers, moved by my example, each gave him a thousand ducats, so my father was left with four thousand ducats in cash, plus another three thousand — the value of the portion that fell to him, which he preferred to keep as land rather than sell. Finally, as I said, we took our leave of him, and of the uncle I mentioned, not without sorrow and tears on both sides. They urged us to send word whenever we had the chance of how we were faring, whether well or badly. We promised we would, and when he had embraced us and given us his blessing, one of us set out for Salamanca, another for Seville, and I for Alicante, where I had heard a Genoese ship was loading a cargo of wool bound for Genoa.

It is now some twenty-two years since I left my father's house, and in all that time, though I have written several letters, I have had no news at all of him or of my brothers. As for my own adventures over that period, I will tell them briefly now. I sailed from Alicante, reached Genoa after a smooth voyage, and went on from there to Milan, where I equipped myself with weapons and a few pieces of a soldier's gear. From there I intended to go and enlist in Piedmont, but when I was already on the road to Alessandria della Paglia, I learned that the great Duke of Alva was on his way to Flanders. I changed my plans, joined him, served under him in the campaigns he fought, was present at the executions of the Counts Egmont and Horn, and rose to the rank of ensign under a famous captain from Guadalajara named Diego de Urbina. Some time after my arrival in Flanders, news came of the league that his Holiness Pope Pius V, of happy memory, had formed with Venice and Spain against the common enemy, the Turk, whose fleet had just captured the famous island of Cyprus, which belonged to the Venetians — a deplorable and disastrous loss. It was known for certain that the Most Serene Don John of Austria, natural brother of our good king Don Philip, was coming as commander-in-chief of the allied forces, and rumors were flying about the enormous preparations for war then underway. All of this stirred my heart and filled me with a longing to take part in the campaign everyone expected; and though I had reason to believe — and very nearly firm promises — that at the first opening I would be promoted to captain, I chose to leave everything behind and make my way, as I did, to Italy. As my luck would have it, Don John had just arrived at Genoa and was continuing on to Naples to join the Venetian fleet, which he later did at Messina. In short, I can say that I took part in that glorious expedition, by then promoted to captain of infantry — an honorable post my good luck, rather than my merits, raised me to. And on that day — so fortunate for Christendom, because on it every nation on earth was cured of the mistaken belief that the Turks were invincible at sea — on that day, I say, when Ottoman pride and arrogance were shattered, among all the men made happy there (for the Christians who died that day were happier than those who survived in victory) I alone was miserable. Instead of the naval crown I might have expected had it been Roman times, on the night that followed that famous day I found myself with shackles on my feet and manacles on my hands.

It happened like this. El Uchali, the king of Algiers, a bold and successful corsair, had attacked and captured the leading Maltese galley, leaving only three knights alive on board, all of them badly wounded. The flagship of John Andrea, which carried me and my company, came to its rescue, and doing what duty demands in such a situation, I leaped aboard the enemy galley. It then sheered away from the ship that had engaged it, which kept my men from following me, and so I found myself alone in the middle of my enemies — too many of them for me to resist. In short, I was captured, covered with wounds. El Uchali, as you know, gentlemen, escaped with his entire squadron, and I was left a prisoner in his hands, the one unhappy man among so many filled with joy, and the one captive among so many freed; for fifteen thousand Christians, all rowing at the oars of the Turkish fleet, regained their long-awaited liberty that day.

They took me to Constantinople, where the Grand Turk, Selim, made my master general at sea, because he had done his duty in the battle and had carried off the standard of the Order of Malta as proof of his bravery. The following year, which was the year seventy-two, I found myself at Navarino, rowing in the flagship with the three lanterns. There I saw, and noted, how the chance to capture the entire Turkish fleet in harbor was thrown away; for all the marines and janissaries on board were so sure they were about to be attacked inside the harbor itself that they had their kits and their pasamaques — their shoes — ready, so they could flee ashore at once without waiting for the assault, such was their terror of our fleet. But Heaven arranged things otherwise — not through any fault or negligence of the general commanding on our side, but because of the sins of Christendom, and because it is God's will and pleasure that we should always have instruments of punishment on hand to chastise us. As it turned out, El Uchali took refuge at Modon, which is an island near Navarino, and putting troops ashore, he fortified the mouth of the harbor and sat tight until Don John withdrew. On that expedition the galley called the Prize was captured, whose captain was a son of the famous corsair Barbarossa. It was taken by the chief Neapolitan galley called the She-wolf, commanded by that thunderbolt of war, that father to his men, that successful and undefeated captain Don Álvaro de Bazan, Marquis of Santa Cruz — and I cannot resist telling you what happened at the capture of the Prize.

The son of Barbarossa was so cruel, and treated his slaves so brutally, that when the men at the oars saw the She-wolf galley bearing down on them and closing the distance, they all dropped their oars at once and seized their captain, who was standing on the platform at the end of the gangway, screaming at them to row harder. Passing him along from bench to bench, from the stern to the bow, they bit him so savagely that before he had been carried much past the mast his soul had already gone to hell — so great, as I said, was the cruelty with which he treated them, and the hatred with which they hated him.

We returned to Constantinople, and the following year, seventy-three, word spread that Don John had seized Tunis, taken the kingdom from the Turks, and installed Muley Hamet in power — ending the hopes that Muley Hamida, the cruelest and bravest Moor in the world, had nursed of returning to rule there. The Grand Turk took the loss bitterly to heart, and with the cunning his whole race possesses, he made peace with the Venetians (who wanted it far more eagerly than he did), and the following year, seventy-four, he attacked the Goletta and the fort that Don John had left half built near Tunis. Through all these events I was laboring at the oar with no hope of freedom; at least I had no hope of winning it by ransom, because I was firmly determined not to write to my father and tell him of my misfortunes. In the end the Goletta fell, and the fort fell too. Arrayed against those positions were seventy-five thousand regular Turkish soldiers, plus more than four hundred thousand Moors and Arabs from every part of Africa, and trailing behind that enormous host came such munitions and engines of war, and so many sappers, that with their bare hands they could have buried the Goletta and the fort under handfuls of earth. The Goletta, until then considered impregnable, fell first — and it fell through no fault of its defenders, who did everything they could and should have done, but because experience proved how easily trenches could be dug in the desert sand there. Water used to be found at a depth of two palms, while the Turks found none at two yards; and so, using a great quantity of sandbags, they raised their earthworks so high that they overlooked the walls of the fort, sweeping them with fire as if from a raised battery, so that no one could make a stand or keep up the defense.

It was a common opinion that our men should not have shut themselves up inside the Goletta but should have waited in the open at the landing place; but those who say so are talking carelessly, with little understanding of such matters. If the Goletta and the fort together held barely seven thousand soldiers, how could so small a force, however determined, march out and hold its ground against enemy numbers like those? And how can anyone avoid losing a stronghold that receives no relief, especially when it is surrounded by a host of determined enemies fighting on their own soil? But many believed — and I believed it too — that it was a special favor and mercy that Heaven showed Spain in allowing the destruction of that breeding ground and hiding place of trouble, that devourer, that sponge, that moth of endless money, wasted there fruitlessly for no purpose except preserving the memory of its capture by the invincible Charles V — as if those stones were needed to make that memory eternal, which it is and always will be. The fort fell too, but the Turks had to win it inch by inch, because the soldiers defending it fought so bravely and stubbornly that the enemy dead in twenty-two general assaults came to more than twenty-five thousand. Of the three hundred defenders who survived, not one was taken without wounds — clear and unmistakable proof of their courage and resolve, and of how sturdily they had defended themselves and held their post. A small fort, or tower, that stood in the middle of the lagoon under the command of Don Juan Zanoguera, a Valencian gentleman and a famous soldier, surrendered on terms. They took prisoner Don Pedro Puertocarrero, commandant of the Goletta, who had done everything in his power to defend his fortress and felt its loss so deeply that he died of grief on the road to Constantinople, where they were carrying him as a prisoner. They also captured the commandant of the fort, a man named Gabrio Cerbellon, a Milanese gentleman, a great engineer and a very brave soldier. Many notable people died in those two fortresses, among them Pagano Doria, a knight of the Order of St. John and a man of generous character, as he showed by his extraordinary openhandedness toward his brother, the famous John Andrea Doria. What made his death sadder still was that he was killed by some Arabs to whom, once he saw the fort was lost, he had entrusted himself, and who had offered to guide him, disguised as a Moor, to Tabarca, a small fort or trading post on the coast held by the Genoese who worked the coral fishery. Those Arabs cut off his head and carried it to the commander of the Turkish fleet, who demonstrated on them the truth of our Castilian proverb that "though the treason may please, the traitor is hated" — for they say he ordered the men who brought him the gift to be hanged for not having brought Doria alive.

Among the Christians captured in the fort was a man named Don Pedro de Aguilar, a native of some town in Andalusia — I do not know which — who had served as ensign in the fort, a soldier of high reputation and rare intelligence, and one who had, in particular, a special gift for what they call poetry. I mention this because his fate brought him to my galley and to my bench, and made him a slave to the same master; and before we left the port this gentleman composed two sonnets as epitaphs, one on the Goletta and the other on the fort. In fact, I might as well recite them, because I know them by heart, and I think they will please rather than displease.

The instant the captive mentioned the name Don Pedro de Aguilar, Don Fernando glanced at his companions, and all three of them smiled; and when he came to the subject of the sonnets, one of them said, "Before your worship goes any further, I beg you to tell me what became of that Don Pedro de Aguilar you have been speaking of."

"All I know," the captive replied, "is that after spending two years in Constantinople, he escaped disguised as an Arnaut, in the company of a Greek spy; but whether he regained his freedom or not, I cannot say — though I suspect he did, because a year later I saw the Greek in Constantinople, but I had no chance to ask him how the journey had turned out."
"Well, you are right," the gentleman answered, "because that Don Pedro is my brother, and he is in our village right now, in good health — rich, married, and the father of three children."
"Thanks be to God for all the mercies he has shown him," said the captive, "because in my opinion there is no happiness on earth that compares with recovering one's lost liberty."
"And what is more," said the gentleman, "I know the sonnets my brother wrote."
"Then let your worship recite them," said the captive, "because you will deliver them better than I could."
"Gladly, with all my heart," said the gentleman. "The one on the Goletta goes like this."
